title: secp256k1-ecdlp: parallel Pollard rho on order-6 classes with a sigma walk, all arithmetic in instructions

claims.statement: For uniform x in [0,r) and input Q=[x]P for the fixed standard secp256k1 generator P, the parallel distinguished-point Pollard rho algorithm in proof.md recovers x with probability at least 0.39. It walks on the order-6 classes given by negation and the GLV endomorphism, using 2^32 walks, 2^16 adders, batched affine additions and deterministic fruitless-cycle escapes. The walk stores actual points and adds the tabulated image sigma(R_i) of each adder, so the class sequence equals the standard canonical walk while no step multiplies by beta; the canonical rotation is decided from 64-bit fixed-point fractions with an exact fallback (Lemma 1). Total computation is at most 2^126.418986 target-group-operation equivalents, including preprocessing, distinguished-point storage and lookup, all failures and restarts, collision replay, verification and output. No reference operation is claimed: each walk step, a batched incomplete affine addition in the package's own 4x64-bit inline-assembly field arithmetic, is charged at most 795 scalar AArch64 instructions at C=1000 (0.795 units), against 781.0 measured with the organizer's Callgrind toolchain on two input sets; the Python replica matches every final point. Peak memory is at most 2^74.74996 bytes. Preprocessing is at most 2^48.619659 units and is included in total work. Nonuniform advice is 0 bytes. This is a classical cold attack on one target with no uncharged advice or quantum steps. The success bound of 0.411523 relies on the disclosed heuristics H1-H3 in proof.md. H1 is the standard random-mapping model for r-adding class walks with an exponent penalty of at most 4/2^16; H2 bounds fruitless-cycle rates; H3 is the representativeness of the measured instruction counts. These are supported by toy-curve experiments with the identical walk and by production-curve measurements, not proved. This is a carefully accounted generic attack, not a claim of a practical break.

experiments.purpose: Run the exact sigma walk from proof.md on random prime-order toy curves y^2=x^3+7 over p = 1 mod 3 (the secp256k1 shape, b=7), or on y^2=x^3+4 subgroups with b=4. The walk uses class keys +-y (as Montgomery representatives, a fixed bijection), the same canonical rule, adder images and index, both cycle rules and escapes, distinguished points and walk abandonment. The run counts all steps to the first useful class collision, solves each instance end to end and checks [x]P=Q, and compares the empirical success curve with 1-exp(-T^2/(2N)). Toy scale only: it tests the H1/H2 collision statistics and says nothing about production cost.

Check Lemma 1 of proof.md on random and edge-case reduced values: the 64-bit fraction approximations g_0 = a_3 and g_1 (4x64-bit limbs) are within [0,1] and [0,8] of floor(2^64*(beta^j x mod p)/p), and the kernel's rule for the canonical rotation either agrees with the exact minimum or falls back to the exact computation.
Recompute the claimed time_log2, preprocessing, memory and success lower bound from the stated parameters with exact integer arithmetic.
